Malala Yousafzai accused of misusing Afghanistan donations, fund’s spending under scrutiny

Afghan-German investigative journalist Zarlashta Daisy Watanmal claims the Malala Fund has not channelled money to organisations in Afghanistan.

Debdutta Chakraborty

15 October, 2026 10:18 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Pakistani activist Malala Yousafzai | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Nobel Prize winner Malala Yousafzai is now being labelled a ‘charity grifter’ on X. An Afghan investigative journalist decided to look into how many schools the Malala Fund had sponsored in Afghanistan, and the numbers did not look good, with the journalist claiming there were none.

Ironically, even as the two countries remain locked in conflict along their border, Pakistanis and Afghans on X found common ground in their anger over whether Malala was a ‘fraudster’.

The allegations were raised by Zarlashta Daisy Watanmal, an Afghan-German investigative journalist and academic, and influencer Nancy Sidley.

Show Full Article

Both questioned the organisation’s public financial disclosures, particularly its ‘Afghanistan Initiative’, the allocation of educational grants, executive compensation, and the relationship between its revenue and expenditure.

Watanmal, in an X post on Tuesday, questioned the Malala Fund’s Afghanistan Initiative, alleging that publicly available financial information did not clearly establish how much funding had been transferred directly to organisations operating inside Afghanistan.

“My initial finding about @MalalaFund: It’s reported that over 10 million $ were awarded by Malala Fund to 57 organisations, majority going to its Afghanistan Initiative. A massive red flag & FRAUD. She spent zero on any Afghanistan-based org nor has she ever been to Afghanistan,” she wrote on X .

Watanmal subsequently said she intended to investigate the matter further. In another post, she wrote:

“We won’t let you walk away @Malala with the millions you raised in the name of Afghan women and girls. We will hold you accountable and I will investigate this fully. I can see zero spending in Afghanistan. Where are your ghost schools and organisations you funded in [Afghanistan]?”

She also claimed to have received hundreds of messages from Afghan women and girls in the country following the emergence of the allegations.

“I’m receiving hundreds of messages since yesterday from Afghan women & girls in Afghanistan. They’re all shocked that @Malala & her father @ZiauddinY made millions under their name while they have no clue nor received a penny. Shame they made millions in our Afghan women’s name,” Watanmal added.

The allegations have intensified debate over whether international organisations supporting education in politically restricted environments should be expected to maintain a direct physical presence in the countries they serve, or whether funding through regional and international partners can constitute meaningful assistance.

Defenders of international nonprofit organisations point out that restrictions imposed by the Taliban authorities in Afghanistan can complicate the delivery of grants and educational services. Under such circumstances, organisations may work through partners operating from neighbouring countries or through external institutions supporting activities inside Afghanistan.

The absence of a directly registered or physically based recipient organisation does not, by itself, establish that no educational assistance has reached people in the country. Conversely, the existence of an international programme does not, on its own, establish that its intended beneficiaries have received the promised assistance.

Financial disclosures, executive pay under scrutiny Sidley, an influencer who said she had reviewed the Malala Fund’s 2024-2025 financial reports, drew attention to a reported difference between the organisation’s annual revenue and expenditure.

According to figures cited by her, the fund recorded approximately $16.48 million in revenue and $23.34 million in total expenses during the reporting period. Its reported net assets stood at approximately $42.97 million, commonly rounded to $43 million.

The difference between reported revenue and expenses was approximately $6.86 million, indicating that the organisation spent more during the year than it received in revenue.

The financial discussion has also focused on the allocation of expenditure across three broad categories: programme services and grants, administration, and fundraising. The reported breakdown puts approximately 82 per cent towards programme services and grants, 10 per cent towards administration, and 8 per cent towards fundraising.

Under this breakdown, the overwhelming majority of spending is classified as supporting the organisation’s programmes and educational initiatives, while administrative and fundraising expenses together account for approximately 18 per cent.

The discussion has also centred on compensation paid to senior personnel and the costs associated with executive travel.

Figures circulated by Sidley and other social media users put the chief executive’s compensation at nearly $372,000, that of a chief adviser at approximately $320,000, and that of the chief operating officer at nearly $241,000.

Amid the heated social media debate, other users pointed to references to first-class or private travel for officers in the financial reporting. They argued that such expenses warranted scrutiny when an organisation raises money in the name of girls who face severe barriers to education.

The Malala Fund is registered in the United States as a public charity based in Washington, DC. The American entity holds the organisation’s principal financial assets and governs its global operations.

The organisation also operates through international affiliates and regional structures, including Malala Fund UK, which is registered with the UK Charity Commission, and a registered international nongovernmental organisation (INGO) branch in Pakistan.

Malala’s public role draws political criticism The controversy has expanded beyond accounting questions into wider disputes over Malala Yousafzai’s public role, the politics of international advocacy, and the use of humanitarian causes in geopolitical messaging.

Ahmad F Samin, a former academic adviser to the World Bank, accused the activist of profiting from the suffering of Afghans.

“While she can’t find Afghanistan on a world map, she has received millions of dollars in the name of the innocent people of Afghanistan. She is not alone; the majority of conflict profiteers have turned the pain and suffering of victims of war into a lucrative business,” he wrote.

Other Afghans also joined the debate. Afghan taekwondo player and women’s rights activist Marzieh Hamidi wrote on X :

“The struggle for Afghanistani women’s rights is much bigger than any one individual. Afghanistani women themselves, alongside countless activists and organizations, have been fighting this battle for decades. Their voices, sacrifices, and achievements must not be overshadowed. Anyone claiming to represent their cause must be held to the highest standards of transparency, accountability, and integrity!”

A Pakistani account, FrameTheGlobe, made a separate political allegation about the origins and purpose of Malala’s public profile.

“Malala’s genuine life-changing event was turned into a Hillary Clinton sponsored influence campaign. A common practice to exercise American soft power in the region,” the account alleged.

Pakistani academic Fareeha Zaheer described Malala as a “native informant”, arguing that her public narrative had helped her gain prominence in the West.

“I knew Malala was a ‘Native Informant’, a girl using her marginalized position to gain fame/ position/status in Global North. Her narrative of oppression perfectly suited the global capitalist Postcolonial Narrative,” Zaheer wrote on X.

French journalist, political analyst and commentator Catherine Perez-Shakdam responded to Watanmal’s allegations by questioning their implications and calling for accountability if they were substantiated.

“My goodness! Did she actually? Can someone enlighten me on this because it is criminal. Women and girls in Afghanistan deserve a lot better than crooks interested in making a few $$$ on their back. If this is true @Malala is condemning millions of innocent women and girls!” she wrote.

The debate also spawned memes. One Pakistani X user shared an image from Mughal-e-Azam with the caption : “ Utho Anarkali, goron ko Malala Fund ka fraud pata chal gaya hai (Wake up, Anarkali, the white people have found out about the Malala Fund fraud).”

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)

Opinion

Pakistan’s Mecca Pact ambition has a problem—too many fronts, too little room

Pakistan’s commitments to Saudi Arabia come as militancy at home, tensions with Afghanistan and ties with Iran constrain Islamabad’s room for manoeuvre.

Sonam Mahajan

15 October, 2026 09:59 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Turkish foreign minister Hakan Firad (centre) and defence ministers, chiefs of general staff of Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in Istanbul on 31 August, 2026 | X @MFATurkiye

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

P akistan has spent years trying to convince the Gulf that it is more than a country looking for economic assistance. Its military ties with Saudi Arabia have long been central to that effort, giving Islamabad strategic influence it has sought to translate into a larger regional role.

The Makkah Pact was meant to do just that, but it comes at a time when Islamabad is already facing mounting security and political pressures at home, even as its commitments to Riyadh could draw it into a wider regional conflict.

Pakistan is stretched across several fronts. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, militant violence continues, while relations with the Afghan Taliban have deteriorated over the presence and activities of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). Islamabad once expected the Taliban’s return to power in Kabul to improve its security environment. Instead, it now accuses Kabul of allowing militants to operate from Afghan territory, a charge Kabul rejects, and the dispute has spilled into cross-border military action. In Balochistan, separatist groups keep attacking security personnel and infrastructure, including projects linked to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor.

Show Full Article

The Makkah Pact, signed in August, has since acquired a more immediate purpose as Saudi Arabia faces growing threats from Yemen’s Houthis. On 5 October, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye agreed to move towards the practical implementation of their collective defence commitments, including the rapid deployment of agreed military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Pakistan was also appointed to provide the alliance’s first secretary-general.

Within days, the risks became more concrete. On 8 October, a double attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed three people. On 10 October, another attack on the airport killed 12 and injured 309. A further strike hit it the following day, killing a Pakistani resident and injuring 11 others. Saudi Arabia’s King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was also targeted. The Houthis renewed warnings to airlines against using Saudi airports and airspace, raising the prospect of further attacks on civilian and economic infrastructure.

Riyadh now faces pressure to respond, and Pakistan’s commitments are being tested in circumstances that could look very different from those envisaged in August. For an army tied down at home, Pakistan has less room to manoeuvre in Saudi Arabia, and in its dealings with Iran, than the pact suggests.

Commitments and Pakistan under pressure For Islamabad, the difficulty is defining what its commitment to Saudi security means in practice. Does collective defence mean protecting Saudi territory, helping intercept incoming missiles and drones, or supporting military operations against the Houthis inside Yemen? Each level of involvement has implications for Pakistan’s relations with Iran and its ability to act as a diplomatic interlocutor.

There is a precedent. In 2015, when Saudi Arabia sought Pakistan’s participation in its military intervention in Yemen, Pakistan’s parliament declined to commit forces. It nevertheless affirmed that Pakistan would stand by Saudi Arabia if the kingdom’s territorial integrity or the holy sites were threatened. Islamabad sought to preserve its relationship with Riyadh without being drawn into a war whose consequences could extend well beyond Yemen.

The calculation is no easier now. The Houthis have declared the kingdom’s airspace a military zone, with only Mecca and Medina as exceptions. If Saudi Arabia faces repeated attacks on its territory, how far can Islamabad limit its role to defensive assistance? And if Saudi operations against the Houthis intensify, can Pakistan continue to restrict its involvement to the defence of the kingdom?

Conflicting reports cloud what Pakistan is already doing. Reuters reported that between 30,000 and 40,000 Pakistani troops had been deployed to Saudi Arabia, citing a Pakistani official. Pakistan’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting rejected the figures and operational details on 6 October as speculative, saying such matters were confidential.

Separately, The New York Times reported that Pakistani fighter jets were being used in strikes against the Houthis. Pakistan dismissed the report as ‘fake and fabricated’. Anyone who has followed Pakistan for long enough knows that when Islamabad is this quick to dismiss a report, it is often worth looking a little closer.

There is a political dimension, too. Reuters has reported that Pakistan agreed to deploy additional troops under the defence arrangement without parliamentary approval. In 2015, by contrast, Parliament publicly debated the risks of involvement in Yemen. Today, operational details remain undisclosed while the military, under Field Marshal Asim Munir, plays a central role in shaping Pakistan’s external commitments. The more consequential the commitment, the harder it becomes to separate questions of military capacity from questions of who is making these decisions and how they will be scrutinised.

The domestic pressure increased on 11 October, when President Asif Ali Zardari suspended the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government led by Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), after the federal government claimed it had failed to contain militancy. PTI condemns the move and is preparing a march on Islamabad. The confrontation risks deepening a political conflict when the state needs a coherent response to militancy.

For the military leadership, the competing demands are clear. The army is expected to contain militancy at home while projecting Pakistan as an indispensable security partner abroad. A larger role in Saudi Arabia could bring Islamabad diplomatic influence and financial benefits. It could also commit the military to a conflict whose duration and costs it cannot control.

Iran and the limits of Pakistan’s balancing act Pakistan has strong reasons to preserve its relationship with Riyadh. But its relationship with Iran is equally important to its security calculations along the western border. Islamabad has tried to maintain ties with Tehran while positioning itself as a mediator between Iran and Washington. That role is already facing questions.

During a visit to Herat in Afghanistan, Iranian parliamentarian Mohsen Zanganeh took a swipe at Pakistan’s efforts to mediate between Tehran and Washington, alleging that even Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s public message on the peace initiative had been written by the Americans. His remarks followed scrutiny of Sharif’s post on X, which initially carried the word ‘Draft’ before it was edited.

Pressure from Washington could make this balancing act harder still. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says that Washington is working with Pakistan and Türkiye to cut off Iran’s overland trade routes. He also says that the US is likely to seize around $1 billion in Iranian-linked cryptocurrency. The implications for Pakistan go beyond diplomacy. The country shares a long border with Iran, where cross-border commerce, including informal trade and fuel smuggling through Balochistan, is deeply entrenched. Shutting down Iran’s overland trade routes would hit commercial interests and informal networks that Pakistan itself has struggled to control.

There is also the question of public opinion. Mohammed bin Salman is an important strategic partner for Pakistan’s military establishment, but that does not mean Pakistanis will view a confrontation with the Houthis in the same light. Iran retains symbolic appeal among sections of Pakistani society because it is seen as one of the few Muslim states still willing to confront Israel and the United States directly. The Houthis, too, attract support from some who view the conflict through that wider lens. Pakistani opinion is neither uniformly pro-Iranian nor pro-Houthi, but the military cannot assume that the strategic preferences of Riyadh and Rawalpindi will translate into popular consensus at home.

Pakistan’s problem, then, is whether it can define the limits of that commitment without undermining its other interests. A role that begins with defending Saudi territory could become harder to contain if the conflict widens, while any involvement in operations against the Houthis would carry consequences for relations with Tehran and for opinion at home.

The Makkah Pact does not mean Pakistan will have to fight in Yemen. That will depend on what Saudi Arabia asks of Islamabad and how far Pakistan is willing to go. But the promise of rapid deployment raises a larger question about how much room Pakistan has to manoeuvre if its partners expect it to act.

Pakistan’s generals want the country to play a larger regional role. The test will be whether they can turn that ambition into influence, while managing competing military and political demands at home and abroad, without taking on commitments that leave Islamabad with fewer choices rather than more.

Sonam Mahajan is a strategic affairs commentator and columnist specialising in Pakistan, Afghanistan, terrorism and the geopolitics of South Asia. She tweets @AsYouNotWish. Views are personal.

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)

Safety of Indian seafarers, tankers raised in Doval’s conversation with Iranian counterpart, says MEA

PTI

14 October, 2026 09:47 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi, Oct 14 (PTI) The issue of safety and security of Indian seafarers and tankers figured in the recent phone conversation between National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei, the Ministry of External Affairs said on Wednesday.

The two sides also discussed regional situation and international developments, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in response to a query during his bi-weekly media briefing.

The telephonic conversation that took place on October 12 focused on the prevailing security situation in West Asia.

Show Full Article

Jaiswal was asked the details about the outcome of the conversation, and if India raised the issue of attacks on Indian-flagged vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Regarding the conversation that our National Security Advisor had with his counterpart in Iran, this conversation happened on October 12. National Security Advisor spoke to the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of Iran, His Excellency Dr Mohsen Rezaei,” he said.

“They discussed bilateral issues. They also discussed regional situation and international developments. And during the meeting, the safety and security of Indian seafarers was raised, as the safety and security of Indian tankers was also raised,” Jaiswal added.

New Delhi has maintained that the repeated attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure in the Gulf are “completely unacceptable and must cease immediately”.

India on Wednesday condemned the string of attacks on civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, saying the “totally unacceptable” acts need to cease immediately.

New Delhi also asserted that it remains committed to doing the best for the welfare and well-being of Indian nationals abroad.

India has been consistently calling for resolution of the West Asia crisis through dialogue and diplomacy.

New Delhi has also been concerned over spate of attacks on merchant ships in the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz.

When asked about the proposed India-US bilateral trade agreement, Jaiswal said External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has spoken about it at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum. Both sides remain engaged on this particular matter for a mutually beneficial bilateral trade agreement, he said.

India and the US are continuing to engage to iron out differences on the proposed trade deal, and negotiations are heading towards a “landing point”, Jaishankar said on Tuesday, while noting that the core fundamentals of the bilateral strategic partnership remain unchanged.

Asked if the H-1B issue and the recent comments made by the US vice president will be raised during US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s upcoming visit to India, Jaiswal just said “several issues of bilateral nature will be discussed”.

Rubio will travel to India next week to further strengthen energy cooperation, the US Department of State said on Tuesday.

Jaiswal was also asked about Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s expected visit to Canada, and whether the bilateral trade deal is likely to be concluded before the visit.

On the trade deal, Jaiswal said the fifth round of negotiations happened in Ottawa a week ago or so, and both sides remain committed to a mutually beneficial Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).

PM Modi, after a telephonic conversation with his Canadian counterpart Mark Carney on Tuesday, said he had a “warm and productive” conversation with him and both leaders agreed to build on the “positive momentum” in bilateral ties.

Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand, who is on a working visit to India, on Wednesday met Modi. The PM said they had a productive discussion on further strengthening India-Canada ties in trade, technology and energy.

Asked about the Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council raising issues related to recent communal incidents, Jaiswal said, “It is our expectation that such issues will be addressed by the Bangladeshi side.”

On the Home Ministers’ Meeting of BIMSTEC here on Tuesday, the MEA spokesperson said, “We had participation from all BIMSTEC countries, and post the conversation, the meeting, a Delhi Declaration was also adopted, wherein the commitment of all the BIMSTEC countries to strengthen cooperation across a range of areas including fight against terrorism, counter-narcotics measures, and anti-money laundering cooperation.”

“It is our expectation that with this inaugural dialogue, there will be a stronger security cooperation among all members,” he said.

On the recent comment made by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) in Geneva over the recent detention of thousands of protesters in Delhi, he reiterated that it was “unwarranted” and at the same time “unacceptable because it amounts to interference” in India’s internal affairs.

They have, it seems, an approach of “extreme selectivity” and if they continue on this path, then obviously, it will lead to loss of faith in multilateralism, Jaiswal said, adding that at the same time, it “undermines their credibility as an organisation”. PTI KND KVK

Airtel’s Mittal says his firm ahead of Musk’s Starlink in India’s Satellite internet queue

PTI

14 October, 2026 08:49 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi, Oct 14 (PTI) Bharti Airtel Chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal on Wednesday said his satellite communications venture Eutelsat OneWeb was significantly ahead of Elon Musk’s Starlink in the queue to launch services in India, adding a fresh twist to a public dispute over regulatory approvals and competition in the country’s satellite internet market.

Meanwhile, government sources, responding to the controversy surrounding Starlink and Musk’s recent claims, said any company operating in India must comply with the law of the land and added that the Centre’s position has been clear and consistent throughout.

“Government’s position has been very clear, and was so even at the time they had applied, that if you don’t follow Indian laws, you cannot do business here…So to do business here you have to follow Indian laws,” sources said.

Show Full Article

At the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026, Mittal said his satcom venture Eutelsat OneWeb is significantly ahead of Elon Musk’s Starlink in the satcom queue in India, having applied five years ago, and added that he would be happy to receive the go-ahead at least a few days before the US tech billionaire.

“I think I am significantly ahead in the queue from him. I applied five years back,” Mittal said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026. “We don’t have the permission, so we’ll be very happy to get it at least a few days before him..

Mittal said OneWeb’s ground network has been ready for three years, and its satellites have been hovering over India for five years, but the company is still awaiting permission to begin commercial operations.

His remarks come after Musk, the world’s richest man, accused powerful business interests of blocking Starlink’s entry into India. In a series of posts on social media platform X last week, Musk took aim at Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani, sarcastically addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and questioning whether he wielded greater influence over India’s decisions than Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Musk has alleged that some business groups are seeking to preserve a “monopolistic chokehold” on Indian consumers. However, the Ministry of Communications has rejected the charge, describing suggestions that the regulatory framework or its application was unfair or discriminatory as “baseless and misconceived”.

The government said satellite operators must meet the same regulatory requirements, including security conditions and spectrum allocation rules, before they can begin commercial services.

Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia said last week that three ventures — Musk’s Starlink, Reliance’s Jio Satcom and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb — had secured satellite communications licences. Amazon’s Project Kuiper has expressed interest but must follow the established procedure, he said.

Scindia had said spectrum would be assigned once the government finalised a revenue-based charging framework and individual operators fulfilled security requirements. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) and the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) were close to a decision on satellite spectrum pricing, he added.

The distinction between a licence and operational approval is central to the dispute: securing a licence does not automatically allow a company to begin commercial services. Spectrum assignment and the fulfilment of security conditions remain key steps.

The dispute comes at a consequential time for Reliance, which is preparing for the planned initial public offering of Jio Platforms, its digital services business. The proposed offering — the biggest so far in India — is expected to open on October 21 and values the company at about USD 106 billion.

Reliance is also developing its satellite ambitions, including a proposed constellation of about 1,600 low-earth-orbit satellites aimed at extending internet connectivity to 600,000 villages. That would put Jio in more direct competition with Starlink, which is seeking access to a vast market where satellite broadband could serve remote communities and locations poorly covered by terrestrial networks.

Ironically, Reliance and SpaceX last year signed an agreement to explore ways of bringing Starlink services to Indian customers through Jio’s retail network.

Reliance’s Jio has already reported 524 million customers and extensive distribution capabilities, giving it a significant advantage in reaching consumers. Starlink, by contrast, would need to establish its customer base and operating model in India while meeting local requirements. PTI MBI ANZ MR
